Standard deviation and Euclidean distance (C backend)

Source: R/core_stats.R
cspread.Rd

csdev() returns the standard deviation of a numeric vector and cdistm() the straight-line (Euclidean) distance between two vectors of the same length. Both run in the package's compiled core, the same code that rmorie and rmoriedata reach through LinkingTo: rmoriebricklayer, so a figure computed here is the figure those packages compute. Use them when you want the shared core's answer rather than base R's, for example when checking a capsule's recorded summary statistics against a fresh computation.

Usage

csdev(x, ddof = 1L)

cdistm(a, b)

Arguments

x, a, b

Numeric (or logical) vectors; coerced with as.numeric(). a and b must have the same length.

ddof

Delta degrees of freedom, a single number; as.integer() truncates it to an integer. The divisor is n - ddof. The default 1 gives the sample standard deviation, matching stats::sd(); 0 gives the population figure.

Value

csdev(): a length-1 numeric, the standard deviation in the units of x (NA when x holds a missing value, NaN when length(x) <= ddof). cdistm(): a length-1 non-negative numeric, the distance in the units of a and b.

Details

csdev() computes $$s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n - \mathrm{ddof}} \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar x)^2},$$ so ddof = 1 is the sample standard deviation of stats::sd() and ddof = 0 the population figure. cdistm() computes \(\sqrt{\sum_i (a_i - b_i)^2}\).

Missing values propagate: there is no na.rm, and one NA makes the result NA. Remove them first (for example with stats::na.omit()) when that is what you want. A vector with no more than ddof values has no defined spread and gives NaN (one value with the default ddof = 1, or an empty vector). Two empty vectors are at distance 0.

Refusals: a character, factor, list or data-frame x, a or b ("must be numeric"), and for cdistm() vectors of different lengths ("must have the same length"). Logical input is accepted and counted as 0/1. Both run in one pass over the data and allocate nothing beyond the coerced input.

See also

cmom() for the mean, variance, skewness and kurtosis in a single pass; cmad() for a spread that one wild value cannot move.

Examples

# Sample standard deviation, matching stats::sd().
csdev(c(2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9))
#> [1] 2.13809
all.equal(csdev(1:10), stats::sd(1:10))
#> [1] TRUE

# ddof = 0 divides by n instead of n - 1.
csdev(1:10, ddof = 0)
#> [1] 2.872281
all.equal(csdev(1:10, ddof = 0), sqrt(mean((1:10 - mean(1:10))^2)))
#> [1] TRUE

# Missing values propagate; remove them first if they should be ignored.
csdev(c(3, NA, 5))
#> [1] NA
csdev(stats::na.omit(c(3, NA, 5)))
#> [1] 1.414214

# Euclidean distance between two points.
cdistm(c(0, 0), c(3, 4))     # 5
#> [1] 5
cdistm(1:5, 1:5)             # 0 -- a point is zero from itself
#> [1] 0

# Vectors of different lengths are refused rather than recycled.
try(cdistm(1:3, 1:2))
#> Error : `a` and `b` must have the same length
